translations.text: Saturn said: "Lo! I have tasted the books of all the islands through their intricate letters, and unlocked the learned arts of Libya and of the Greeks, as well as the histories of the kingdom of the Indians.
The commentators guided me to accounts in the great books [?] hard [?].
Yet in all those ancient writings I have never been able to find the truth gathered together.
I still wanted to find out what the palm-twigged Pater Noster was like in mind or majesty, in courage or wealth or nobility."

I will give you all of it, son of David, lord of the Israelites: thirty pounds of pure gold and my twelve sons, if you bring me to the point where I am inspired by the words of the canticle, Christ's line,
and satisfy me with the truth. Then I will go away safe and set out as I wish on the back of the water, over the river Chebar, to seek the Chaldeans."

Solomon said: "Wretched on earth, useless in his life and empty of wisdom, is the man who cannot praise Christ through that canticle. He wanders like a beast, like field-roaming cattle without understanding.
He wanders full of wind. On Doomsday the devil, the terrible dragon, will shamefully hurl him from a dark sling with iron apples. All of them have grown from the heads of the [?] of reproach.
Then he would rather have had any knowledge at all of that canticle than all this bright creation, filled from the ground up with molten gold and silver, its four corners full of treasures.
Then he is base and estranged from the Lord almighty, and he wanders alone, unlike the angels."
Saturn said: "But which of all creatures can most easily open the holy door of the kingdom of heaven brightly, in due number [?]?"
Solomon said: "The palm-twigged Pater Noster opens the heavens, gladdens the holy, makes the Creator merciful, strikes down murder, quenches the devil's fire and kindles the Lord's.
Likewise, with that bright prayer you can make the blood boil, the devil's gore, so that its drops rise, strengthened [?] by sweat,
seven times more terribly than the bronze cauldron when it boils most greedily over the grip of the coals for the frailties of twelve men.
For the canticle has the most widely famous word of all Christ's books. It teaches the scriptures, directs with its voice, keeps its own place in the kingdom of heaven, and carries war-gear."

Saturn said: "But what kind of canticle is it that should be practised with mindfulness by one whose spirit wishes to soften against deadly sin, to be gladdened [?] out of sorrow, and to be separated from his sins?
Truly, the Creator gave it a glorious form. Curiosity about this very often questions me in the world, hurries away, and troubles my mind.
No man, no hero under the heavens, knows how my mind sinks, busy with books. At times a burning rises in me, and my mind wells up fiercely near my heart."
Solomon said: "God's saying is golden, studded with gems, and it has silver leaves. Through the grace of the Spirit, each of them can separately speak the gospel.
It is the wisdom of the mind [?], the honey of the soul, and the milk of the spirit, the most blessed of glories.
It can fetch the soul out of the endless night under the earth. The fiend can never fasten it down there with fetters so firmly
that it does not break his craft and tear apart all his cunning devices, even if he locks it in with fifty bars.
It ravages hunger, plunders hell, overthrows the surging fire, and builds up glory.
It is mightier than the world and stronger in its foundation than the grip of all the stones.

It is the physician of the lame and the light of those who blink in blindness. It is also the door of the deaf, the tongue of the dumb, the shield of the guilty, the Creator's hall, the ferryman of the flood, the saviour of the people, the guardian of the waves, the [?] of poor fishes and of serpents, the forest of wild beasts, the guardian in the wilderness, and the enclosure of honours.
And whoever is eager to sing God's word truly, and will always love it without sin, can [?] the hateful spirit,
[...] put the fighting fiend to flight, if you first bring down on him from above the prologa prima, whose name is P (rune ᛈ).
The warrior has a long rod, a golden goad, and with a strong mind he keeps whipping the fierce fiend. A follows him in his track with overwhelming might and strikes him down as well.
T injures him and stabs him in the tongue, wrenches his throat [?], and breaks his cheeks.
E harms him, as he always wants to stand firm against every one of the fiends.

Then R, the prince of letters, angrily seeks him out against his will. He quickly seizes the fiend by the hair and lets flint break the demon's shanks. He has no regard for the joints of his limbs, and he is no good physician to him.
Then he turns himself away under the clouds and seeks a place of refuge, covered by darkness. Indeed, woe is at his heart when, hanging there, he longs for hell, that narrowest of homelands.
Then the twins of the church, N and O together, spurn him. Each of them brings whips on the way. For a while they torment the alien body of flesh, but they do not mourn for its life.
Then S comes, the leader of angels, the staff of glory. He seizes the wrathful fiend by the feet and dashes his face forward onto the hard stone, scattering his teeth throughout the host of hell.
Each of them hides himself in the gloom of the shadow. The ravager is afflicted; Satan's thane is utterly silenced.

Likewise Q and V lay him low in death, bold chieftains. They go against him with light spears, long shafts and fierce whips. They do not hold back their blows, their hard strokes. The devil is hateful to them.
When I and L and the angry C gird him about with battle (the curved letter fights with bitter terror), the captive of hell soon gives way, so that he retreats backward.

When F and M crowd around him from outside, the guilty ravager, they have sharp spears, a terrible flight of arrows. They let fire and arrows scatter onto the fiend's hair, a bitter terror. They pay the slayer back harshly and grimly, and so they often break his boasting.

Then at last the cunning G (rune ᛄ) closely restrains him. God sends G to help his friends. After him comes D (rune ᛞ), full of five powers. Fire [?] is the third letter, near the road, waiting quietly.
H hurries on. An angel equips him, Christ's warrior, in living garments, the young raiment of one who follows God [?].

Then the life-twins in the air, under the hosts of the stars, rage fiercely at him with the points of rods and with silver whips, until his bones gleam and his veins bleed. They pour spear-fury on the greedy devil.
Through a man's mouth, God's saying can always put every one of the fiends to flight for any man, and it can afflict the black host of the wicked, however strangely they may shift in their colours.

In place of a body of bone they take on a coat of feathers; sometimes they seize seafarers. Sometimes they change into the body of a strong and prickly serpent. It stings beasts and plunders the livestock that roam the fields.
Sometimes he drives a horse down into the water and gores it with horns, until its heart's blood, a foaming bath in the flood, runs down to the ground.

Sometimes he fetters a doomed man and makes his hands heavy when he must fight for his life in battle against a hostile troop. He writes a heap of death-marks on the man's weapon, baleful letters, and puts a curse on the blade and on the glory of the sword.
Therefore no man should often draw out the edge of his weapon thoughtlessly, even though its beauty pleases him. Instead, he must always sing
the Pater Noster when he draws his sword, and pray joyfully to the palm-tree that it may give him both life and hand when his enemy comes."
"[...] deceive, before he knows the truth, that the sinful souls will be stuck with the enemies in the middle of hell.
Then the high King will command that hell be shut, full of fire, with the fiends in it."
Then the wise son of David had overcome and refuted the nobleman of the Chaldeans.
Yet the one who had come from his journey, having travelled from afar, was in good spirits. Never before had his heart laughed.
Listen! I have heard that in days of old, wise-minded men, leaders of the world, contended and disputed about their wisdom. Whoever lies or denies the truth does worse.
Solomon was more renowned, though Saturn, a bold leader, held some of the keys of books, the locks of learning.

He had travelled through every land: the sea of India, the Corsias [?] in the east, the kingdom of the Persians, Palestine, the city of Nineveh, and the Predan [?] in the north, the treasure-halls of the Medes, the land of Marculf, the kingdom of Saul, as it lies to the south around Gilboa and to the north around Geador [?],

The hall of the Philistines, the stronghold of the Greeks, the forest of the Egyptians, the water of the Medes, the cliffs of Horeb, the kingdom of the Chaldeans, the crafts of the Greeks, the race of Arabia, the learning of Libya, the land of Syria, Bithynia, Batanaea [?],
Pamphylia, the border of Porus, Macedonia, Mesopotamia, Cappadocia, Christ's homeland, Jericho, Galilee, Jerusalem [?] "... or I keep silent and think about what is useful, though I do not speak."
I know, then, that if you go across the Wendel Sea, over the river Chebar, to seek your homeland, you will want to boast that you have overcome and confounded the children of men.
I know that the Chaldeans were very boastful in battle, very proud of their gold and very arrogant about their glories, where the many [?] came together south around the plain of Shinar.
Tell me about the land where no man can set foot."
Saturn said: "That famous one was called Wolf, the surging seafarer, known among the peoples of the Philistines, a friend of Nimrod.

In that field he slew [twenty-five] dragons at dawn, and then death fell upon him. Therefore no man can visit that land, that boundary-place, no bird can fly there, and no beast of the earth can reach it either.
From there the race of poisonous creatures was first awakened far and wide. Now, surging, they force their way in with venomous breath.
His sword still shines, badly broken [?], and the hilts gleam over the graves."

Solomon said: "A man is foolish if he goes into deep water when he cannot swim and has no sailing ship and no bird's flight, and cannot touch the bottom with his feet. Indeed, such a man tests God, the Lord's powers, very foolishly."
Saturn said: "But what is the dumb thing that rests in a certain valley?
He is very wise and has seven tongues. Each tongue has twenty points, and each point has the wisdom of an angel, whichever one of them he chooses to bring up,
so that you see the walls of golden Jerusalem gleaming and their rood of joy [?] shining, the sign of the righteous. Say what I mean."
Solomon said: "Books are glorious. They often proclaim the certain will to anyone who thinks at all.
They strengthen and establish steadfast thought, and cheer the mind of every man out of the distress of this life."
Saturn said: "Bold is he who tastes the craft of books; he who has command of them is always the wiser."
Solomon said: "They send victory to every righteous person, a haven of salvation, to those who love them."

Saturn said: "There is one matter in this worldly kingdom that my curiosity has troubled me about for [fifty] years, by day and by night, through the depths of creation. My mourning spirit still does so, until the eternal Lord grants that a wiser man settle it for me."
Solomon said: "What you say is true. I will quickly explain to you about the wondrous creature. Do you want me to tell you?
A bird sits in the middle borderlands of the Philistines. A mountain surrounds it, a broad golden wall.
The wise men of the Philistines guard it eagerly. They fear something that will never happen: that a whole people will take it from them by the edges of weapons.
They are wary of this, and every night they guard it, north and south, on two sides, with two hundred guards.
The bird has four heads of middle-sized [?] men, and in the middle it is like a whale; it has a vulture's feathers and a griffin's feet; it lies fast in fetters and looks fierce,

It beats about violently and rattles its trappings. It cries out mournfully and soothes its grief. It writhes in its torment, lives without joy, and sings strangely. Its limbs are seldom ever at rest.
It longs hard. It seems to it that it will be three [thirty] thousand winters before it hears the din of Doomsday.

No one of earthly kind on the land knew of it until I alone found it and then ordered it to be bound beyond the broad water. So the proud son of Melot, the chief of the Philistines, ordered it to be bound fast and locked in fetters as a protection against terror for the people.
Those who dwell far off, the chiefs of the Philistines, call that bird 'vasa mortis.'"
Saturn said: "But what is that wonder that travels throughout this world, goes about sternly, beats at foundations, rouses tears, and often comes this way to fight?
Neither star nor stone nor the bright gem, neither water nor wild beast, can escape it in any way. Instead, into its hand go hard and soft, great and small.
Every year, three times thirteen thousand in number of those who dwell on the ground, those who fly in the air, and those who swim in the water must go to it as food."
Solomon said: "Old age has power over everything on earth; with a plundering war-fetter, a broad chain, a long line, she reaches far and subdues [?] everything she wants.
She breaks the tree and breaks off its branches, shakes the standing trunk in its course and fells it to the ground; after that she devours the wild bird.
She overcomes the wolf, she outlasts stones, she overcomes steel, she bites through iron with rust, and she does the same to us."
Saturn said: "But why does the snow fall and cover the earth, hide the shoots of plants, bind the fruits, crush and oppress them, so that for a time they are shrivelled with cold?

Very often he also tests a multitude of wild beasts. He bridges over the waters, breaks the gate of cities, travels boldly, and plunders" [?] "much more strongly than the stronger malice that leads him to the hateful dwelling with the dangerous fiend, as the fiend wishes."
Saturn said: "Night is the darkest of weathers, need is the hardest of fates, sorrow is the heaviest burden, sleep is most like death."
Solomon said: "For a little while leaves are green; then they turn yellow again, fall to the earth and wither, and turn to dust.

So then those fall who have long persisted in sins, who live in wickedness, hide great treasures, and guard them eagerly in a stronghold, as the fiends wish. And the heedless ones expect that the King of glory, almighty God, the eternal, will hear them."
Saturn said: "It will soon be seen, once the wave is allowed to flow over all the land. When its time comes, it will never stop that journey until it hears the din of Doomsday."
Solomon said: "Then woe will come to these proud men who now live longest here in wickedness in this passing creation.
Your people showed that long ago; they strove against the Lord's might, and therefore they did not finish that work.
Yet I shall not anger you, brother. You are of a very bitter kind, angry, of a mighty race. Do not run into that malicious nature!"
Saturn said: "Tell me, King Solomon, son of David, what are the four ropes of the doomed man?"
Solomon said: "Fates that have come to pass: these are the four ropes of the doomed man."
Saturn said: "But who then will judge the Lord Christ on the Day of Judgement, when he judges all creatures?"
Solomon said: "Who then dares to judge the Lord, the Saviour, who made us from dust, out of the wound of night [?]? But tell me what were the things that did not exist."
Saturn said: "But why may the sun not shine brightly throughout all the wide creation? Why does it leave mountains and moors, and many waste places as well, in shadow? How does that come about?"

Solomon said: "But why were earthly riches not all shared out alike among peoples? One man has too little and is greedy for goods. Because of what he has earned, God sets him among the blessed for rest."
Saturn said: "But why are those companions, weeping and laughter, together at the same time? Very often they tear apart the happiness of those who are eager for honour. How does that come about?"
Solomon said: "Wretched and despondent is the one who always laments in sorrow; he is most hateful to God."
Saturn said: "Why then may we not all go straight into God's kingdom in glory?"
Solomon said: "The grip of fire and the chill of frost, snow and sun, cannot live together or last out their lives together. Whichever of them has less strength must bow and yield."
Saturn said: "But why then does the worse man live longer?
The worse man knows no greater honour in this worldly kingdom among his kinsmen and friends."
Solomon said: "No one can put off the costly [?] journey for any length of time; he must endure it."
Saturn said: "But how does that come about, for good or for evil? When two twins are born of one woman, their glory is not alike.
One is wretched on earth; the other is blessed and very fortunate among the nobles of the people. One lives a little while, fails in this wide creation, and then departs again in sorrow.
I ask you, lord Solomon, which of them has the better lot?"
Solomon said: "When a mother bears a son, she does not decide how his long journey through the world will be shaped for him.
Often she raises a child to misfortune, to her own sorrow, when he later endures his hardships in the hour of battle.
His mother must often and repeatedly weep bitterly for her son when he goes out young, with a wild mind, a weary heart and a sorrowful spirit, and often slips,
weary, without joys, deprived of glory; sometimes, sad at heart, he keeps watch over the hall and lives far from his people; his own lord often looks away from the wretched man.
Therefore, when a mother bears a son, she has no power over the child's prosperity. Instead, one must follow another by birth; that is the ancient ordering of things."
Saturn said: "But why will a man not eagerly earn for himself in his youth precious lordship and the doing of deeds, wade into wisdom, and strive after understanding?"
Solomon said: "Listen! A fortunate nobleman can easily choose in his mind a gracious lord, a prince, for himself. The wretched man cannot do so."
Saturn said: "But why does this water strive throughout the kingdom of the world, this deep creation endure [?]

It may not rest by day; it presses on at night and draws along by its power; it christens and cleanses a multitude of the living and makes them beautiful with glory. I do not know at all why the stream may not be still at night."
[?] the embrace of its life. It is always obedient to its teachers. Very often it also humbles the devil's host, where a multitude of wise men is gathered.
When a morsel slips away from a wise man and he sees it by the light, he bends down after it, blesses it, seasons it, and eats it himself.
So that one morsel, if it is blessed, is much better for every man to eat, if he knows how to think about it, than for him to have seven days of feasting.
Light has the hue and form of the Holy Spirit, the nature of Christ; it very often makes that known.
If fools keep it for any length of time without restraint, it rages through the roof, breaks and burns the buildings, and hovers high and wide, [?]
it rises at length, climbs by its nature, and tries to find out when the fire may go back to its first creation in the Father's dwellings, back to its homeland, from where it came before.
It is wholly visible to a man who knows how to share out the Lord's torch, because there is no kind of living creature [?]
neither bird nor fish nor stone of the earth, nor the surge of water nor the branches of the wood, nor mountain nor moor nor this world, but that it is from now on of the nature of fire."

Saturn said: "Very often I have heard wise men of old speak and swear about a certain matter: which of two things was without doubt the stronger, fate or foresight, when they often contend with each other in their violence, and which of them tires first.

I know it for a truth. The wise men of the Philistines told me long ago, when we sat in disputation, spread out books and laid them on our laps, mingled our discourses and took up many of them, that there was no man on earth who could track down the answer to the doubt between those two."
Solomon said: "Fate is hard to change, and it surges very often. It stirs up weeping, it heaps up woe, it harms the spirit, it carries the year,
and yet a wise-minded man can moderate every fate, if he is shrewd of mind and is willing to seek help from his friends, and also to enjoy the divine spirit."

Saturn said: "But what does mighty fate ordain for us, the beginning of all sins, mother of feud, root of woes, head of weeping, father and mother of every original sin, daughter of death? And why does she dwell among us?
[?] Listen! While living, it will be slow to grow weary, so that it does not breed feud through the strife of crimes."

Solomon said: "The fellowship of the blessed angel and the proud one would not stay together in God's kingdom. One obeyed his Lord; the other began to make for himself, through secret arts, a banner and a broad coat of mail,

[He] said that he and his companions would plunder the whole kingdom of the heavens and then sit beside Him as an equal half-sharer, and breed [?] for himself with the tenth part, until he did not know the end of his anger through [?].
Then the Prince of the nobler ones was troubled by the devil's thoughts;
so He let him fall down from the height, threw him down beneath the regions of the earth, and ordered him bound fast there. Those are the ones who fight against us.
Therefore every wise man has more cause for weeping.

When the blessed Lord of angels found that they would no longer accept teaching from Him, He cast him out of glory and drove them far and wide, and He commanded them, the children of the heaven-dwellers, that they too must dwell forever, as long as they lived, in the surging fire,

suffer weeping and lamentation under the heavens. And He made hell for them, a deadly cold dwelling covered over with winter, and sent into it water and serpent-pits, many a terrible beast with iron horns,

bloody eagles and pale adders, thirst and hunger and fierce strife, terrors to the eyes, sorrow; and each of these hardships stands against them eternally, without any reversal, for as long as they live."

Saturn said: "Is there then on this earth any man of earthly race, of those one has [?], whom death would wait for before the day comes when his allotted term has run out and he is summoned out at once?"

Solomon said: "To every man the Lord of the heavens sends an angel when the day begins; the angel must watch over where the man's mind wants to go, so that he grows eagerly in God's will and is mindful of the Creator's glory while it is day.
Then two spirits surround him: one is brighter than gold, the other is blacker than the abyss; one comes from over the steel hell;
one teaches him to keep love, the mercy of the Creator, and the counsel of his kinsmen; the other incites him and leads him into harm, points out and reveals to him the misdeeds of poor men,
and through that sharpens his mind, leads him and lures him and entices him throughout the land, until his awe, full of malice, has turned to anger because of the guilt of poor men.
So then the fiend fights in four ways, until, through the devil's deeds, he turns to the worse side for the length of a day and does the will of the one who entices him into wrong.
Then the angel departs weeping, travelling away to his homeland, and tells all of it: 'I could not force the hard steel stone out of the heart; it is stuck in the middle of him.'"
